bib.title: Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug

read.skipped: Appendix few-shot exemplar bodies (E.1-E.5, F.1-F.6, G.1-G.4) skimmed by header and samples: long repetitive schemas/code; the chat prompts E.6-E.7, F.7-F.10, G.5-G.8 read in full.

question: Can a pretrained LLM, with only few-shot prompting, debug its own generated code using execution results and self-written code explanations?
hypothesis: Explaining code line by line (rubber duck debugging) lets the model find its own errors, and richer feedback including unit test execution helps debugging; the authors also hypothesize better code explanation yields better debugging.
contributions: SELF-DEBUGGING: few-shot prompting that teaches an LLM to debug its predicted program with no training
Rubber duck debugging via code explanation without human feedback or error messages
State-of-the-art on Spider, TransCoder and MBPP at time of writing
Improved sample efficiency: matches or beats baselines sampling more than 10x candidates

method.summary: A pretrained code LLM generates a program, the program is executed, the model explains it (or traces it) and a feedback message is formed from the explanation plus execution/unit-test results; the loop repeats until the feedback says correct or 10 turns. Evaluated with Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and StarCoder on three tasks, with no fine-tuning.
method.task: code generation: text-to-SQL (Spider dev), C++-to-Python translation (TransCoder), text-to-Python (MBPP)

datasets.name: Spider (dev set)
datasets.split: development set; no unit tests; prompt includes one row per table
datasets.preprocessing: returned table truncated to first 2 rows in the prompt

datasets.name: TransCoder (C++ to Python)
datasets.split: test set; all unit tests visible in the prompt

datasets.name: MBPP test set
datasets.split: first unit test in the prompt, other 2 hidden for evaluation

inference.decoding: initial generation: greedy (temperature 0) from one program; multiple samples at temperature 0.7 then execution-based majority vote; all explanations, feedback and revised programs use greedy decoding
inference.temperature: 0 (single program, and all debugging steps); 0.7 (multiple samples)
inference.samples: 1 greedy program, or n samples (Spider 1/8/16/32; TransCoder 1/5/10/25; MBPP n=10 in Table 1b); no repeated runs or seeds reported
inference.prompting: few-shot for Codex/StarCoder (Spider baseline 5-shot, simple and explanation feedback 9-shot; TransCoder baseline 3-shot, feedback 2-shot; MBPP baseline 3-shot, simple/UT 6-shot, UT+Expl 3-shot); 0-shot chat prompts with system 'You are an expert programming assistant.' for GPT-3.5/GPT-4

parameters.selection: among samples without execution errors, pick the program with the most frequent execution result; programs failing visible unit tests are filtered first
parameters.mbpp_success_branch: after a program passes the visible test, one extra 'Is the code above correct? If not, please fix it.' turn; the revision is used only if it also passes the visible test

other.stopping: terminates when feedback says the prediction is correct, or max turns
other.TransCoder debugging: applied only if the Python fails the unit tests, so no model-predicted feedback
other.Fig 6a read from figure: Spider Codex baseline by samples 1/8/16/32 = 77.5/78.7/80.7/81.3; self-debugging = 80.8/82.5/82.9/84.1 (read from Fig 6a; these match the Table 2a Codex 81.3 and 84.1, so those are inferred to be the 32-sample setting)

metrics.name: Spider accuracy
metrics.definition: execution accuracy on Spider dev (not further defined in the text)

metrics.name: TransCoder pass@1
metrics.definition: fraction of 560 problems whose Python passes all 10 unit tests

metrics.name: MBPP accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of 500 problems passing all 3 unit tests (1 visible, 2 hidden)

eval.protocol: single run per cell, no seeds, intervals or significance tests reported

availability.data: Spider, TransCoder, MBPP public; full prompts in Appendices E-G

prompts.text:
System: You are an expert programming assistant.
User: Write the SQL query for the given question.
<insert the database schema and the question here>
Assistant: <chatGPT Completion>
User: Does the SQL match the question? If not, generate the fixed SQL.

System: You are an expert programming assistant.
User: Summarize the return type of the SQL execution.
<insert the database schema and the SQL here>
Assistant: <chatGPT Completion>
User: Infer the return type of the question.
<insert the question here>
Assistant: <chatGPT Completion>
User: Does the SQL match the question? If not, generate the fixed SQL.
The SQL prediction above is correct!

User: Translate the C++ code into Python code. Please respond with code only (with the code inside a Markdown code block).
<insert C++ program here>
... User: The Python translation does not do the same thing as the C++ code. These are the results of one failed unit test that tests whether the Python translation's outputs match the C++ program's outputs:
<insert one failed unit test and its execution result here>
Correct the Python translation.

User: Complete the following task in Python:
<insert problem here (includes one unit test)>
... User: The code above fails the given unit test:
<insert the failed unit test and its execution result here>
Please fix the Python code.
Explain the Python code line by line.

evidence.quote: All experiments for SELF-DEBUGGING use greedy decoding to generate code explanations, feedback messages and new programs. We set the maximum number of debugging turns to be 10

results.claim: Unit-test execution plus code explanation lifts Codex on TransCoder by about 12 points
results.setup: TransCoder 560 problems, Codex, greedy initial program, UT + Expl feedback, max 10 turns

results.claim: GPT-4 gains over 12 points on TransCoder and 8 on MBPP; gain on par with Codex
results.setup: TransCoder, GPT-4, UT + Expl, 0-shot chat prompts
results.quote: its self-debugging performance gain is on par with Codex: over 12% improvement on Transcoder, and 8% improvement on MBPP

results.claim: GPT-4 on MBPP with unit-test feedback
results.setup: MBPP 500 problems, 1 visible and 2 hidden tests, GPT-4, UT feedback

results.claim: On Spider (no tests) simple feedback does not help Codex; explanation feedback helps
results.setup: Spider dev, Codex; Simple = 81.3 equal to baseline; setting inferred to be 32 samples (Fig 6a)
results.note: Table 2a does not say how many samples; Fig 6a lists 81.3 and 84.1 at 32 samples.

results.claim: Without unit-test execution, Codex on MBPP is worse with simple self-judged feedback than with no debugging
results.setup: MBPP, Codex, self-debugging with no code execution, simple feedback

results.claim: Without execution, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are overconfident in their initial predictions
results.setup: Table 3, no unit test execution, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4
results.quote: Without unit test execution, both models tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions, while GPT-4 is better than GPT-3.5 on Python generation.

results.claim: Without execution, GPT-4 improves MBPP by 3.6 points and other benchmarks by about 1
results.setup: GPT-4, MBPP, no unit-test execution
results.quote: GPT-4 without unit test execution improves the MBPP accuracy by 3.6%

results.claim: Without execution, Codex still improves by up to 5 points; trace feedback consistently beats simple
results.setup: Codex, TransCoder and MBPP without unit-test execution
results.quote: With Codex, SELF-DEBUGGING still improves the performance by up to 5%, and the execution trace feedback consistently improves over the simple feedback performance.

results.claim: Self-debugging from greedy decoding matches 16-sample baseline on Spider; from 8 samples beats the 32-sample baseline
results.setup: Spider dev, Codex, execution-based majority vote
results.quote: applying SELF-DEBUGGING to predictions generated with greedy decoding matches the baseline accuracy using 16 samples, and SELF-DEBUGGING from 8 samples outperforms the baseline accuracy using 32 samples

results.claim: Improvement after the first debugging turn on Spider is within 0.1 points
results.setup: Spider, Codex
results.quote: typically one debugging turn is sufficient, and the accuracy improvement after one turn is within 0.1%

results.claim: Extra-hard Spider problems gain 9 points (63.9 to 72.9)
results.setup: Spider dev by hardness, Codex; read from Fig 6b
results.quote: on extra hard problems, SELF-DEBUGGING increases the accuracy by 9%

results.claim: Codex self-debugging beats prior prompting and trained rerankers on Spider
results.setup: Spider dev, Codex + Expl.
results.note: baseline_value is LEVER (trained verifier); Coder-Reviewer 74.5, MBR-Exec 75.2, T5-3B reranking 80.6

results.claim: Codex self-debugging at n=10 samples beats MBR-Exec, Reviewer (n=25) and LEVER (n=100) on MBPP
results.setup: MBPP, Codex, UT + Expl., from 10 samples
results.note: LEVER 68.9 at n=100; Codex without debugging 72.2 at n=10

results.claim: StarCoder (15.5B) gains about 6 points on MBPP with trace feedback
results.setup: MBPP, StarCoder
results.quote: i.e., 6% on MBPP with the execution trace feedback

results.claim: Spider: GPT-4 is worse than Codex at initial SQL generation and self-debugging
results.setup: Spider dev, GPT-4 Simple feedback
results.note: paper's guess: GPT-4 is tuned for zero-shot and follows few-shot exemplars less well

results.claim: Successful fixes on TransCoder/MBPP are mostly output mismatches
results.setup: MBPP with gpt-4 (Transcoder with gpt-3.5-turbo: 61.9)
results.table: Table 4b, row Output mismatch, column MBPP

results.claim: Most common Spider errors fixed are wrong WHERE conditions
results.setup: Spider, code-davinci-002

results.claim: Fewer exemplars fit when explanation is added on MBPP, which weakens the explanation gain
results.setup: MBPP UT+Expl prompt has 3 exemplars vs 6 for simple/UT
results.quote: prompts with both simple and unit test feedback messages include 6 exemplars, while the prompt with both the unit test execution and code explanation has 3 exemplars

results.claim: Code explanation of the C++ input alone, without debugging, gives a 2-3 point gain on TransCoder
results.setup: TransCoder, Codex, different numbers of samples
results.quote: leveraging code explanation alone without SELF-DEBUGGING also provides a consistent performance gain of 2 −3% for different numbers of samples

results.claim: Codex baseline on TransCoder vs earlier systems (pass@1)
results.setup: TransCoder, Codex w/o debugging vs TransCoder 44.5, PaLM 51.8, PaLM-Coder 55.1

results.claim: GPT-3.5 zero-shot Spider
results.setup: Spider, GPT-3.5, greedy zero-shot (few-shot 71.1)
results.quote: GPT-3.5 achieves an accuracy of 59.9% with zero-shot prompting, and 71.1% with few-shot prompting

limits: Single run per cell, no seeds, intervals or significance tests reported.
Only 3 benchmarks of short functions; Spider, TransCoder and MBPP are not repository-scale.
Hidden-test evaluation only on MBPP (2 of 3 tests); TransCoder shows all 10 tests to the model, so debugging against them is evaluated on the same tests.
Without execution feedback gains are small and sometimes negative; GPT-3.5/GPT-4 overconfident.
GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 evaluated with 0-shot chat prompts, Codex with few-shot, so the model comparison mixes prompt styles; GPT-4 worse on Spider.
Code-davinci-002 (Codex) has been deprecated by OpenAI (not stated in the paper).
Preliminary result only: model-generated feedback about semantic errors adds nothing over line-by-line explanation.
Cost in tokens or turns is not reported; sample efficiency counts programs only.
